claim: NUDT21-spanning copy-number variations (CNVs) are associated with intellectual disability.
source: We previously showed that NUDT21-spanning copy-number variations (CNVs) are associated with intellectual disability (Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: Patients with NUDT21-spanning CNVs have other genes included in their copy-number variations.
source: However, the patients' CNVs also included other genes.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from prior work.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have 50% reduced Nudt21 mRNA.
source: We found that although these mice have 50% reduced Nudt21 mRNA, they only have 30% less of its cognate protein, CFIm25.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have only 30% less CFIm25 protein despite 50% reduced Nudt21 mRNA.
source: We found that although these mice have 50% reduced Nudt21 mRNA, they only have 30% less of its cognate protein, CFIm25.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have learning deficits.
source: Consistent with what we observed in the deletion patients, we found that Nudt21 heterozygosity is sufficient to cause learning deficits in mice in a variety of behavioral assays.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have cortical hyperexcitability.
source: Further, it causes cortical hyperexcitability and misregulated APA in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by EEG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have misregulated alternative polyadenylation (APA) in their hippocampi.
source: Further, it causes cortical hyperexcitability and misregulated APA in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A 30% reduction of CFIm25 in human stem cell-derived neurons induces APA misregulation in hundreds of genes.
source: This induced APA and protein level misregulation in hundreds of genes, a number of which cause intellectual disability when mutated.
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data from human neurons shown in Figure 6.

claim: A 30% reduction of CFIm25 in human stem cell-derived neurons induces protein level misregulation in hundreds of genes.
source: This induced APA and protein level misregulation in hundreds of genes, a number of which cause intellectual disability when mutated.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from human neurons shown in Figure 6.

claim: Disruption of NUDT21-regulated APA events in the brain can cause intellectual disability.
source: Altogether, these results show that disruption of NUDT21-regulated APA events in the brain can cause intellectual disability.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined mouse and human neuron data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The brain is acutely sensitive to the dose of numerous proteins.
source: The brain is acutely sensitive to the dose of numerous proteins, such that even small perturbations in their levels can cause neurological disease.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Small perturbations in protein levels can cause neurological disease.
source: The brain is acutely sensitive to the dose of numerous proteins, such that even small perturbations in their levels can cause neurological disease.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Proteins that affect the expression of other genes are particularly critical for neurological function.
source: Proteins that affect the expression of other genes, such as transcriptional or translational regulators, are particularly critical (De Rubeis et al., 2014; Vissers et al., 2016; Yin and Schaaf, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FMR1 is an RNA-binding protein that underlies fragile X syndrome.
source: Canonical examples of such broad regulators are the RNA-binding protein FMR1, which underlies fragile X syndrome, and the chromatin modulator MeCP2, whose loss or gain respectively causes Rett syndrome or MECP2-duplication syndrome (Amir et al., 1999; Pieretti et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Pieretti et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991).

claim: MeCP2 is a chromatin modulator whose loss causes Rett syndrome.
source: Canonical examples of such broad regulators are the RNA-binding protein FMR1, which underlies fragile X syndrome, and the chromatin modulator MeCP2, whose loss or gain respectively causes Rett syndrome or MECP2-duplication syndrome (Amir et al., 1999; Pieretti et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Amir et al., 1999).

claim: Gain of MeCP2 causes MECP2-duplication syndrome.
source: Canonical examples of such broad regulators are the RNA-binding protein FMR1, which underlies fragile X syndrome, and the chromatin modulator MeCP2, whose loss or gain respectively causes Rett syndrome or MECP2-duplication syndrome (Amir et al., 1999; Pieretti et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Amir et al., 1999).

claim: Nearly 70% of human genes have multiple polyadenylation sites.
source: Nearly 70% of human genes have multiple polyadenylation [poly(A)] sites, usually within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the mRNA, allowing for transcript isoforms with different 3′ UTR lengths and content (Derti et al., 2012; Hoque et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Derti et al., 2012; Hoque et al., 2013).

claim: Multiple polyadenylation sites are usually within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the mRNA.
source: Nearly 70% of human genes have multiple polyadenylation [poly(A)] sites, usually within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the mRNA, allowing for transcript isoforms with different 3′ UTR lengths and content (Derti et al., 2012; Hoque et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Derti et al., 2012; Hoque et al., 2013).

claim: Longer 3′ UTRs contain additional regulatory motifs for miRNA and RNA-binding protein binding sites.
source: The general implication is that longer 3′ UTRs contain additional regulatory motifs for miRNA and RNA-binding protein binding sites.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: As cells differentiate, pathway-specific mRNAs increasingly use distal polyadenylation sites.
source: In general, as cells differentiate, pathway-specific mRNAs increasingly use distal polyadenylation sites, while cells that are more proliferative use more proximal poly(A) sites (Hoque et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2009; Sandberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Hoque et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2009; Sandberg et al., 2008).

claim: Proliferative cells use more proximal poly(A) sites.
source: In general, as cells differentiate, pathway-specific mRNAs increasingly use distal polyadenylation sites, while cells that are more proliferative use more proximal poly(A) sites (Hoque et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2009; Sandberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Hoque et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2009; Sandberg et al., 2008).

claim: Average 3′ UTR length increases throughout neurogenesis.
source: In the brain, average 3′ UTR length increases throughout neurogenesis, and mature, post-mitotic neurons have the longest average 3′ UTR length of any cell type (Guvenek and Tian, 2018; Miura et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Guvenek and Tian, 2018; Miura et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: Mature, post-mitotic neurons have the longest average 3′ UTR length of any cell type.
source: In the brain, average 3′ UTR length increases throughout neurogenesis, and mature, post-mitotic neurons have the longest average 3′ UTR length of any cell type (Guvenek and Tian, 2018; Miura et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Guvenek and Tian, 2018; Miura et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: Neuronal mRNA 3′ UTR lengths are modulated by activity.
source: Moreover, neuronal mRNA 3′ UTR lengths are modulated by activity and vary between distinct cellular compartments (Tushev et al., 2018), suggesting that cleavage site selection in neurons needs to be carefully regulated and APA dysfunction could cause neurological symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Tushev et al., 2018).

claim: Neuronal mRNA 3′ UTR lengths vary between distinct cellular compartments.
source: Moreover, neuronal mRNA 3′ UTR lengths are modulated by activity and vary between distinct cellular compartments (Tushev et al., 2018), suggesting that cleavage site selection in neurons needs to be carefully regulated and APA dysfunction could cause neurological symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Tushev et al., 2018).

claim: NUDT21 is among the most consequential genes that regulate APA.
source: Numerous genes regulate APA, but NUDT21 is among the most consequential (Gruber et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014; Tian and Manley, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Gruber et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014; Tian and Manley, 2017).

claim: NUDT21 encodes CFIm25, a component of the mammalian cleavage factor I (CFIm) complex.
source: NUDT21 encodes CFIm25, a component of the mammalian cleavage factor I (CFIm) complex (Kim et al., 2010; Rüegsegger et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kim et al., 2010; Rüegsegger et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2011).

claim: CFIm25 binds UGUA sequences in pre-mRNA.
source: CFIm25 binds UGUA sequences in pre-mRNA and the CFIm complex helps recruit the enzymes required for cleavage and polyadenylation (Brown and Gilmartin, 2003; Rüegsegger et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Brown and Gilmartin, 2003; Rüegsegger et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: The CFIm complex helps recruit the enzymes required for cleavage and polyadenylation.
source: CFIm25 binds UGUA sequences in pre-mRNA and the CFIm complex helps recruit the enzymes required for cleavage and polyadenylation (Brown and Gilmartin, 2003; Rüegsegger et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Brown and Gilmartin, 2003; Rüegsegger et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: UGUA binding sites are often enriched at the distal polyadenylation sites of NUDT21-regulated RNAs.
source: The UGUA binding sites are often enriched at the distal polyadenylation sites of NUDT21-regulated RNAs, so CFIm25 typically promotes the synthesis of longer mRNA isoforms (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: CFIm25 typically promotes the synthesis of longer mRNA isoforms.
source: The UGUA binding sites are often enriched at the distal polyadenylation sites of NUDT21-regulated RNAs, so CFIm25 typically promotes the synthesis of longer mRNA isoforms (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: When NUDT21 expression is reduced, proximal cleavage sites are more frequently used.
source: Thus, when NUDT21 expression is reduced, proximal cleavage sites are more frequently used.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of CFIm25 function.

claim: CFIm25 downregulation in multiple human and mouse cell lines typically causes 3′ UTR shortening in hundreds of genes.
source: CFIm25 downregulation in multiple human and mouse cell lines typically causes 3′ UTR shortening in hundreds of genes, and a consequent increase in protein levels of a subset of those genes; however, there are numerous exceptions to these trends (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gennarino et al., 2015; Gruber et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gennarino et al., 2015; Gruber et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014).

claim: CFIm25 downregulation causes a consequent increase in protein levels of a subset of genes.
source: CFIm25 downregulation in multiple human and mouse cell lines typically causes 3′ UTR shortening in hundreds of genes, and a consequent increase in protein levels of a subset of those genes; however, there are numerous exceptions to these trends (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gennarino et al., 2015; Gruber et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gennarino et al., 2015; Gruber et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014).

claim: MECP2 is among the most affected genes in cell-line studies of CFIm25 downregulation.
source: Notably, MECP2 is among the most affected genes in these cell-line studies, and slight perturbations in MeCP2 levels cause neurological disease (Chao and Zoghbi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chao and Zoghbi, 2012).

claim: Slight perturbations in MeCP2 levels cause neurological disease.
source: Notably, MECP2 is among the most affected genes in these cell-line studies, and slight perturbations in MeCP2 levels cause neurological disease (Chao and Zoghbi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chao and Zoghbi, 2012).

claim: NUDT21 is a highly constrained gene.
source: Moreover, NUDT21 is a highly constrained gene.
evidence: This is supported by gnomAD data cited in the manuscript.

claim: In gnomAD of ~140,000 putatively healthy individuals, 125 missense and 13 loss of function variants would be expected in NUDT21 if loss of function were not pathogenic.
source: In the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) of ~140,000 putatively healthy individuals, 125 missense and 13 loss of function variants would be expected in NUDT21 if loss of function were not pathogenic.
evidence: This is supported by citation to gnomAD data (Lek et al., 2016).

claim: In gnomAD, there are only 15 missense and zero loss-of-function variants in NUDT21.
source: Instead, there are only 15 missense and zero loss-of-function variants, suggesting that NUDT21 loss of function is incompatible with health (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to gnomAD data (Lek et al., 2016).

claim: Nine individuals with NUDT21-spanning duplications have intellectual disability.
source: Combining results from our previous work with data from the Decipher database, we have identified nine individuals with NUDT21-spanning duplications that have intellectual disability, and two patients with deletions that have both intellectual disability and seizures (Firth et al., 2009; Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the Decipher database (Firth et al., 2009; Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: Two patients with NUDT21-spanning deletions have both intellectual disability and seizures.
source: Combining results from our previous work with data from the Decipher database, we have identified nine individuals with NUDT21-spanning duplications that have intellectual disability, and two patients with deletions that have both intellectual disability and seizures (Firth et al., 2009; Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the Decipher database (Firth et al., 2009; Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: The duplication patients have three other genes common to their copy-number variations.
source: However, the duplication patients also have three other genes common to their copy-number variations (CNVs) and the deletion patients have nearly 20 common genes (Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: The deletion patients have nearly 20 common genes in their CNVs.
source: However, the duplication patients also have three other genes common to their copy-number variations (CNVs) and the deletion patients have nearly 20 common genes (Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: CFIm25 is expressed in neuronal (NeuN positive) nuclei in the cortex and hippocampus.
source: Thus, we first sought to confirm that mice express Nudt21 in the brain, and found CFIm25 in neuronal (NeuN positive) nuclei in regions important for learning and memory—the cortex and hippocampus (Figure 1A & B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: No non-neuronal brain cells visualized expressed CFIm25 at high enough levels to be detected by immunostaining.
source: Notably, no non-neuronal brain cells visualized expressed CFIm25 at high enough levels to be detected by immunostaining (Figure 1A & B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Nudt21 knockout mice were generated by excising exons two and three.
source: Next, we generated Nudt21 knockout mice by excising exons two and three, which removes the RNA-binding domain of CFIm25 and induces a frame shift mutation leading to nonsense-mediated decay of the transcript (Figure 1C; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic and sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Excising exons two and three of Nudt21 removes the RNA-binding domain of CFIm25.
source: Next, we generated Nudt21 knockout mice by excising exons two and three, which removes the RNA-binding domain of CFIm25 and induces a frame shift mutation leading to nonsense-mediated decay of the transcript (Figure 1C; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Yang et al., 2011).

claim: Excising exons two and three of Nudt21 induces a frame shift mutation leading to nonsense-mediated decay of the transcript.
source: Next, we generated Nudt21 knockout mice by excising exons two and three, which removes the RNA-binding domain of CFIm25 and induces a frame shift mutation leading to nonsense-mediated decay of the transcript (Figure 1C; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Yang et al., 2011).

claim: Complete loss of CFIm25 is embryonic lethal.
source: We crossed the Nudt21+/- mice with each other and observed that of the 32 pups born, there were no homozygous null offspring, showing that complete loss of CFIm25 is embryonic lethal (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the breeding data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have a normal life span.
source: Finally, we found that the Nudt21+/- mice had a normal life span, but consistently weighed ~10% less than their wild-type littermates, indicating that Nudt21 heterozygosity might cause some abnormalities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice consistently weighed ~10% less than their wild-type littermates.
source: Finally, we found that the Nudt21+/- mice had a normal life span, but consistently weighed ~10% less than their wild-type littermates, indicating that Nudt21 heterozygosity might cause some abnormalities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by weight data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice froze on average ~50% less often than their wild-type littermates when exposed to the reinforcement sound cue during conditioned fear training.
source: Their initial fear learning was attenuated: when exposed to the reinforcement sound cue played again two minutes after the initial tone-shock pairing during training, they froze on average ~50% less often than their wild-type littermates (Figure 2Ai).
evidence: This is supported by conditioned fear assay data shown in Figure 2Ai.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice froze on average ~30% less in contextual and cued fear tests.
source: Furthermore, the following day, they froze on average ~30% less in both tests, indicating that Nud21+/- mice have reduced memory of the chamber and the sound cue compared to their wild-type littermates (Figure 2Aii and iii).
evidence: This is supported by conditioned fear assay data shown in Figure 2Aii and iii.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice were not hyperactive in the open field assay.
source: We found that the Nud21+/- mice were not hyperactive, thus validating the conditioned fear results by showing they are not confounded by hyperactivity, and showing that partial loss of Nudt21 function does cause cognitive defects (Figure 2Bi).
evidence: This is supported by open field assay data shown in Figure 2Bi.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice spent ~15% more time in the exposed, center part of the open field.
source: Intriguingly, the Nud21+/- mice spent ~15% more time in the exposed, center part of the open field, which suggests they have reduced anxiety and shows that they have neuropsychiatric features beyond learning and memory deficits (Figure 2Bii).
evidence: This is supported by open field assay data shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice required more time to locate the platform during Morris water maze training trials.
source: We found that the Nudt21+/- mice indeed have spatial learning deficits. On average, they required more time to locate the platform during their training trials, despite swimming slightly faster and covering a greater distance (Figure 2Ci and ii).
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze data shown in Figure 2Ci.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice swam slightly faster and covered a greater distance in the Morris water maze.
source: We found that the Nudt21+/- mice indeed have spatial learning deficits. On average, they required more time to locate the platform during their training trials, despite swimming slightly faster and covering a greater distance (Figure 2Ci and ii).
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze data shown in Figure 2Cii.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice spent ~30% less time in the correct quadrant during the Morris water maze probe trial.
source: Moreover, when we removed the platform, the Nudt21+/- mice spent ~30% less time in the correct quadrant (Figure 2Ciii and iv).
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze probe trial data shown in Figure 2Ciii and iv.

claim: Nudt21+/- mice have significantly more EEG spikes in their frontal cortex relative to their wild-type littermates.
source: Despite a lack of detectable seizures in Nudt21+/- mice, we found significantly more EEG spikes in their frontal cortex relative to their wild-type littermates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by EEG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nudt21 haploinsufficiency is alone sufficient to cause cortical hyperexcitability.
source: This result indicates that Nudt21 haploinsufficiency is alone sufficient to cause cortical hyperexcitability, and suggests that NUDT21 loss of function might increase seizure risk.
evidence: This is inferred from the EEG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 20 genes have significantly different poly(A) site distributions in Nudt21+/- mice compared to wild-type.
source: Moreover, 20 genes have significantly different poly(A) site distributions despite the effects of neuronal CFIm25 reduction being diluted by mRNA from the glia (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Nudt21+/- and wild-type mice separate by principle component analysis of poly(A) site usage.
source: Overall, the genotypes separate by principle component analysis (PCA) when looking at global poly(A) site distribution, showing that the APA consequences of Nudt21 heterozygosity in mice are reproducible (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nudt21+/- and wild-type mice separate by PCA of the proteome.
source: Likewise, PCA shows a separation between the genotypes when looking at the whole proteome by quantitative mass spectrometry (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Of the 20 genes with measurable APA changes in whole-hippocampal lysate, five were detected by mass spectrometry and had protein level changes.
source: Lastly, of the 20 genes with measurable APA changes in whole-hippocampal lysate, five were detected by mass spectrometry and had protein level changes, including Ddx6 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: All protein level changes in genes with APA changes follow the trend where protein levels increase with mRNA shortening.
source: Although there are too few data points to perform a statistical analysis, all observations follow the trend seen in cell lines, where protein levels increase with mRNA shortening.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Human neurons infected with shNUDT21 have a 40% reduction of NUDT21 mRNA.
source: Like the whole-brain extracts from Nudt21+/- mice, the human neurons had a 30% reduction of CFIm25 protein, despite a greater reduction of NUDT21 mRNA (Figure 5A & B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human neurons infected with shNUDT21 have a 30% reduction of CFIm25 protein.
source: Like the whole-brain extracts from Nudt21+/- mice, the human neurons had a 30% reduction of CFIm25 protein, despite a greater reduction of NUDT21 mRNA (Figure 5A & B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is homeostatic stabilization of CFIm25 in human neurons.
source: This difference shows that there is also homeostatic stabilization of CFIm25 in human neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between mRNA and protein reduction shown in Figure 5.

claim: NUDT21 loss of function results in the 3′ UTR shortening of MECP2 in human neurons.
source: Similar to data observed in the NUDT21 CNV patient lymphoblasts, NUDT21 loss of function also results in the 3′ UTR shortening of MECP2 in human neurons, as well as other genes strongly regulated by NUDT21 in cancer-cell-line assays, such as VMA21 and PAK1 (Figure 6Aii-iv; Chu et al., 2019; Gennarino et al., 2015; Masamha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 6Aii and citation to prior work (Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: NUDT21 loss of function results in the 3′ UTR shortening of VMA21 in human neurons.
source: Similar to data observed in the NUDT21 CNV patient lymphoblasts, NUDT21 loss of function also results in the 3′ UTR shortening of MECP2 in human neurons, as well as other genes strongly regulated by NUDT21 in cancer-cell-line assays, such as VMA21 and PAK1 (Figure 6Aii-iv; Chu et al., 2019; Gennarino et al., 2015; Masamha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 6Aiii and citation to prior work (Masamha et al., 2014).

claim: NUDT21 loss of function results in the 3′ UTR shortening of PAK1 in human neurons.
source: Similar to data observed in the NUDT21 CNV patient lymphoblasts, NUDT21 loss of function also results in the 3′ UTR shortening of MECP2 in human neurons, as well as other genes strongly regulated by NUDT21 in cancer-cell-line assays, such as VMA21 and PAK1 (Figure 6Aii-iv; Chu et al., 2019; Gennarino et al., 2015; Masamha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 6Aiv and citation to prior work (Chu et al., 2019).

claim: NUDT21 loss in neurons predominantly results in shorter mRNAs.
source: Overall, NUDT21 loss of function in neurons, similar to other cell lines, causes widespread dysregulation of alternative polyadenylation, predominantly resulting in mRNA shortening (Figure 6C; Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gruber et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 6C and citations to prior work (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gruber et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014).

claim: 129 misregulated genes in NUDT21-depleted neurons have a gnomAD probability of loss-of-function intolerance over 0.9.
source: Of the misregulated genes, 129 have a gnomAD probability of loss-of-function intolerance over 0.9, 26 cause intellectual disability when mutated, and of those, nine are autosomal or X-linked dominant (Supplementary file 1; Lek et al., 2016; McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cross-referencing PAC-seq data with gnomAD (Lek et al., 2016).

claim: 26 misregulated genes in NUDT21-depleted neurons cause intellectual disability when mutated.
source: Of the misregulated genes, 129 have a gnomAD probability of loss-of-function intolerance over 0.9, 26 cause intellectual disability when mutated, and of those, nine are autosomal or X-linked dominant (Supplementary file 1; Lek et al., 2016; McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cross-referencing PAC-seq data with published genetic studies (McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).

claim: Nine misregulated genes in NUDT21-depleted neurons that cause intellectual disability are autosomal or X-linked dominant.
source: Of the misregulated genes, 129 have a gnomAD probability of loss-of-function intolerance over 0.9, 26 cause intellectual disability when mutated, and of those, nine are autosomal or X-linked dominant (Supplementary file 1; Lek et al., 2016; McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cross-referencing PAC-seq data with OMIM (McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019).

claim: NUDT21 loss results in shorter mRNAs and increased protein for many genes.
source: Most commonly, NUDT21 loss results in shorter mRNAs and increased protein, such as with MeCP2, VMA21, and PAK1, which respectively had protein-level increases of 40%, 90%, and 100% (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MeCP2 protein levels increased by 40% in NUDT21-depleted neurons.
source: Most commonly, NUDT21 loss results in shorter mRNAs and increased protein, such as with MeCP2, VMA21, and PAK1, which respectively had protein-level increases of 40%, 90%, and 100% (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: VMA21 protein levels increased by 90% in NUDT21-depleted neurons.
source: Most commonly, NUDT21 loss results in shorter mRNAs and increased protein, such as with MeCP2, VMA21, and PAK1, which respectively had protein-level increases of 40%, 90%, and 100% (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PAK1 protein levels increased by 100% in NUDT21-depleted neurons.
source: Most commonly, NUDT21 loss results in shorter mRNAs and increased protein, such as with MeCP2, VMA21, and PAK1, which respectively had protein-level increases of 40%, 90%, and 100% (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Control and shNUDT21-infected human neurons separate by PCA of differentially expressed genes.
source: We performed principle component analyses (PCA) on mRNA level and cleavage site counts of reads and confirmed that the genotypes separated (Figure 4B and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 7A and D; Yalamanchili et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Only two genes have significant changes in both APA and expression in NUDT21-depleted neurons.
source: Interestingly, altered APA had almost no direct effect on mRNA levels: only two genes have significant changes in both APA and expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression analysis.

claim: 21 differentially expressed genes in NUDT21-depleted neurons have a pLI >0.9.
source: 21 of the DEGs have a pLI >0.9, and four are currently associated with ID (Supplementary file 1; Lek et al., 2016; McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cross-referencing differential expression data with gnomAD (Lek et al., 2016).

claim: Four differentially expressed genes in NUDT21-depleted neurons are currently associated with intellectual disability.
source: 21 of the DEGs have a pLI >0.9, and four are currently associated with ID (Supplementary file 1; Lek et al., 2016; McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cross-referencing differential expression data with published genetic studies (McKusick-Nathans Institute of Genetic Medicine and Johns Hopkins University, 2019; Vissers et al., 2016).

claim: Control and shNUDT21-infected human neurons segregate by PCA of the proteome.
source: When analyzing all proteins, PCA shows a segregation by genotype, revealing that reduced NUDT21 has a notable downstream effect on the entire neuronal proteome (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Many of the NUDT21-regulated genes in neurons are the same as those seen in cancer-line studies.
source: While we did not previously know the consequences of NUDT21 loss in post-mitotic neurons, we found that many of the NUDT21-regulated genes are the same as those seen in cancer-line studies, and the majority follow the same trends.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with prior cancer cell line studies.

claim: Partial loss of NUDT21 function in neurons broadly causes 3′ UTR shortening and increased protein levels.
source: Partial loss of NUDT21 function in neurons broadly causes 3′ UTR shortening and increased protein levels that in turn leads to widespread transcriptomic and proteomic dysregulation, ultimately demonstrating the constitutive function of this gene in various cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the PAC-seq and mass spectrometry data from human neurons.

claim: A partial loss of Nudt21 function causes learning deficits, cortical hyperexcitability, and APA and proteomic misregulation in mice.
source: Here we show that a partial loss of Nudt21 function causes learning deficits, cortical hyperexcitability, and APA and proteomic misregulation in mice.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral, EEG, PAC-seq, and mass spectrometry data from mice.

claim: Partial loss of NUDT21 function in human neurons broadly disrupts gene expression via widespread misregulated alternative polyadenylation and protein levels.
source: Further, we show in human neurons that partial loss of NUDT21 function broadly disrupts gene expression via widespread misregulated alternative polyadenylation and protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by the PAC-seq and mass spectrometry data from human neurons.

claim: Partial loss of NUDT21 function causes intellectual disability.
source: Alongside our previous discovery that patients with NUDT21-spanning deletions have intellectual disability and gnomAD data that NUDT21 is a highly constrained gene, our results provide strong evidence that partial loss of NUDT21 function causes intellectual disability (Gennarino et al., 2015; Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined mouse, human neuron, patient, and gnomAD data.

claim: Individuals with missense variants in NUDT21 that affect its function may have intellectual disability.
source: Because a relatively small reduction in CFIm25 protein was sufficient to cause deficits, these data suggest that individuals with missense variants in NUDT21 that affect its function may also have intellectual disability.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings that a 30% reduction causes deficits.

claim: Duplications of NUDT21 should lead to comparable dysregulation of alternative polyadenylation and protein levels.
source: Moreover, duplications of NUDT21, which we previously showed are associated with ID, should lead to comparable dysregulation of alternative polyadenylation and protein levels, including reduced MeCP2, and thus cause disease (Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculated based on the mechanism of NUDT21 function and prior patient data (Gennarino et al., 2015).

claim: A 30% reduction of CFIm25 protein in the mouse brain was sufficient to cause learning deficits.
source: A mere 30% reduction of CFIm25 protein in the mouse brain was sufficient to cause learning deficits, and mice are neurologically less sensitive to genetic insult than humans (Tan and Zoghbi, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data from Nudt21+/- mice and citation to prior work (Tan and Zoghbi, 2019).

claim: Mice are neurologically less sensitive to genetic insult than humans.
source: A mere 30% reduction of CFIm25 protein in the mouse brain was sufficient to cause learning deficits, and mice are neurologically less sensitive to genetic insult than humans (Tan and Zoghbi, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Tan and Zoghbi, 2019).

claim: Many genes associated with neurodevelopmental diseases encode proteins that regulate or affect transcription.
source: Further, many genes associated with neurodevelopmental diseases encode proteins that regulate or affect transcription (De Rubeis et al., 2014; Vissers et al., 2016; Yin and Schaaf, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (De Rubeis et al., 2014; Vissers et al., 2016; Yin and Schaaf, 2017).

claim: NUDT21 broadly affects alternative polyadenylation and protein levels.
source: NUDT21 adds another dimension to this group of genes insofar as it broadly affects alternative polyadenylation and protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by the PAC-seq and mass spectrometry data from the manuscript.

claim: Neurons are particularly sensitive to protein-level disequilibrium.
source: As a group, these genes demonstrate how a partial loss or gain of function can result in large effects, and further show that neurons are particularly sensitive to protein-level disequilibrium.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that small changes in CFIm25 cause significant deficits.

claim: The observed 40% increase of MeCP2 protein likely contributes to the symptoms seen in the NUDT21 CNV patients.
source: Lastly, while the observed 40% increase of MeCP2 protein likely contributes to the symptoms seen in the NUDT21 CNV patients, the dysregulation in neurons following NUDT21 loss is so widespread that there are probably other mediators of the patients' condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data showing MeCP2 increase and knowledge of MeCP2's role in disease.

claim: Patient symptoms most likely result from the additive effects of numerous misregulated genes.
source: Most likely, patient symptoms result from the additive effects of numerous misregulated genes, especially those that are ID associated.
evidence: This is speculated based on the widespread dysregulation observed in NUDT21-depleted neurons.

claim: Normalization of CFIm25 levels is the most viable molecular therapeutic strategy for treating NUDT21-associated disease.
source: This then points to normalization of CFIm25 levels as the most viable molecular therapeutic strategy for treating this disease.
evidence: This is speculated based on the finding that widespread dysregulation results from CFIm25 reduction.

claim: >90% of filtered PAC-seq reads map to the 3′ UTR.
source: To strengthen the validity of our analysis, we assessed the location of our poly(A) site calls within the gene, and found that >90% are in the 3′ UTR region as expected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by read distribution data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CFIm25 binding motif, UGUA, is enriched upstream of the distal cleavage site in NUDT21-regulated mRNAs that shorten after NUDT21 knockdown.
source: As predicted, we found an enrichment of the UGUA sequence upstream of the distal cleavage site in NUDT21-regulated mRNAs that shortened after NUDT21 knockdown, almost no difference in UGUA frequency upstream of proximal and distal cleavage sites in mRNAs not regulated by NUDT21, and a slight UGUA enrichment upstream of the proximal cleavage site in those mRNAs that lengthened after NUDT21 knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by motif frequency analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is almost no UGUA frequency difference between proximal and distal cleavage sites in mRNAs not affected by NUDT21 loss.
source: As predicted, we found an enrichment of the UGUA sequence upstream of the distal cleavage site in NUDT21-regulated mRNAs that shortened after NUDT21 knockdown, almost no difference in UGUA frequency upstream of proximal and distal cleavage sites in mRNAs not regulated by NUDT21, and a slight UGUA enrichment upstream of the proximal cleavage site in those mRNAs that lengthened after NUDT21 knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by motif frequency analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a slight UGUA enrichment upstream of the proximal cleavage site in NUDT21-regulated mRNAs that lengthen after NUDT21 loss.
source: As predicted, we found an enrichment of the UGUA sequence upstream of the distal cleavage site in NUDT21-regulated mRNAs that shortened after NUDT21 knockdown, almost no difference in UGUA frequency upstream of proximal and distal cleavage sites in mRNAs not regulated by NUDT21, and a slight UGUA enrichment upstream of the proximal cleavage site in those mRNAs that lengthened after NUDT21 knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by motif frequency analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ddx6 is a gene highly expressed in neurons and associated with autosomal dominant intellectual disability.
source: For example, the Nudt21+/- mice express more of the short isoform and less of the long isoform of Ddx6, a gene highly expressed in neurons and associated with autosomal dominant intellectual disability (Figure 4Ai; Balak et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Balak et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: Nudt21+/- mice express more of the short isoform and less of the long isoform of Ddx6.
source: For example, the Nudt21+/- mice express more of the short isoform and less of the long isoform of Ddx6, a gene highly expressed in neurons and associated with autosomal dominant intellectual disability (Figure 4Ai; Balak et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data shown in Figure 4Ai.
